analysis.one_liner: Restores strict bank oversight rules for large and regional banks that were relaxed in 2018.
analysis.headline: The bill to restore stricter bank oversight was introduced with 68 cosponsors but never received a committee vote or House floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in 2023, this bill would have rolled back part of the 2018 law that loosened rules on mid-sized banks. It would require banks with $50 billion or more in assets to follow strict federal standards — stress tests, limits on borrowing, cash reserves, and plans for winding down safely — down from the current $250 billion threshold, and would extend some testing to banks as small as $10 billion. The idea is to catch risky banks early so their failures do not trigger bailouts backed by taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers and taxpayers. If banks holding between $50 billion and $250 billion must pass stress tests and hold cash buffers, failures like Silicon Valley Bank's become less likely — and the ones that do happen are less likely to require government rescues funded by the public. Deposit insurance protects small account holders, but a bank failure still disrupts payrolls, loans, and local economies that ordinary people depend on.

how_it_helps.text: It lowers the threshold for mandatory enhanced standards — stress tests, leverage limits, liquidity requirements, and 'living will' resolution plans — from $250 billion to $50 billion in assets, so regional banks must again prove they can fail without a taxpayer bailout.

It requires company-run stress tests down to $10 billion in assets and adds a third supervisory stress-test scenario, giving regulators and the public an earlier look at weaknesses like the interest-rate and liquidity problems that felled Silicon Valley Bank.
It lowers the threshold for mandatory risk committees from $50 billion to $10 billion, putting dedicated board-level risk oversight at more mid-sized banks.

analysis.who_pays: Regional and mid-sized banks, which would face higher compliance costs from stress testing, liquidity requirements, risk committees, and resolution planning. Those costs can be passed on to borrowers through slightly higher loan rates or fees.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Title IV would re-impose compliance costs — stress testing, liquidity requirements, risk committees — on regional banks with assets as small as $10 billion, which critics argued could push lending costs up and push smaller banks toward consolidation.

The bill was an all-or-nothing repeal of Title IV rather than a recalibration, restoring the strictest thresholds ($10 billion for stress tests and risk committees) rather than the intermediate $50 billion level, the approach its opponents favored.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be meaningfully lower odds of bank failures that spill onto taxpayers and depositors, at a real cost: more compliance burden on mid-sized banks, which could mean slightly costlier or scarcer credit in some communities. Whether that trade is worth it is the core dispute; the bill offered no grandfathering or tailoring, which made the costs more serious than they needed to be.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a vote, or floor action.

narrative.text: The House referred the bill to the Financial Services Committee on March 14, 2023, and no further action was ever taken on it.
No markup, hearing, or vote was scheduled before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Regional and large banks that benefit from the lighter 2018-era rules, since the tighter oversight never advanced; also the committee leadership that kept it off the agenda.

for.name: Rep. Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 14, 2023, days after the Silicon Valley Bank failure, to restore stricter bank oversight.

for.name: 68 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all Democrats, including members like Jayapal, Khanna, Raskin, and Ocasio-Cortez.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 14, 2023 and took no further action — no markup, hearing vote, or floor report — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 68 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so no cross-party support or opposition was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Regional and mid-sized banks ($50B–$250B in assets)
industries.note: The bill restores mandatory stress testing, liquidity rules, and risk committees for banks this size, raising compliance costs — the same rules banks lobbied to shed in 2018. Ordinary people bear the cost when such banks fail; this bill would put that burden back on the banks.

industries.industry: Bank holding companies and nonbank financial companies
industries.note: Larger financial firms lose the discretionary, lighter-touch supervision they gained in 2018 and must meet enhanced prudential standards at lower size thresholds.
The bill revises the supplemental leverage ratio applied to custodial banks and the treatment of certain municipal obligations, a narrower technical adjustment whose effects depend on implementation.

industries.industry: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation / taxpayer-backed deposit fund
industries.note: The bill reduces the likelihood of rare but enormous bailout draws like the 2023 SVB rescue by requiring banks to maintain buffers and resolution plans.
